long_term.hypothesis: The uranium market is entering a multi-year structural bull phase driven by an irreducible supply gap, accelerating nuclear capacity growth (414 operational units with China and India expanding aggressively), and a global energy security imperative that makes nuclear indispensable for decarbonization. The Bridgewater All-Weather signal reads OPTIMAL — falling real yields plus a weak dollar is the textbook environment for commodity outperformance, and uranium's unique supply inelasticity (7-10 year mine development timelines) means the deficit cannot be resolved quickly even at $90+ spot prices.

Supply inelasticity: even with Kazakhstan trending UP, the 16 Mlbs structural deficit requires new greenfield mines that take 7-10 years to permit and build — Kazatomprom already cut 2025 guidance by 17%

data.contrarian_view: This entire thesis collapses if small modular reactors (SMRs) face regulatory delays and cost overruns that kill the nuclear renaissance narrative, or if a Fukushima-scale accident occurs at any global facility, instantly reversing political support and utility contracting momentum. Additionally, if secondary supply from underfeeding, MOX recycling, or government stockpile releases exceeds estimates by 20-30 Mlbs, the vaunted supply deficit disappears and spot could retrace to $60-70.
data.dalio_verdict: In the Bridgewater All-Weather framework, this is a textbook environment for commodity allocation. We are in a falling real yield regime (0.03%) with a weakening dollar (DXY 8th percentile over 2 years) — this is the quadrant where real assets historically outperform financial assets. Uranium fits perfectly as a non-yielding commodity with structural supply constraints, functioning as both an inflation hedge and a geopolitical optionality play. The commodity supercycle regime at 85% confidence reinforces this. However, the risk-parity discipline demands we acknowledge that uranium equities have already moved 30%+ in 90 days and technical signals are deteriorating (multiple SELL signals, flow drought). The Dalio approach would be to maintain strategic overweight exposure sized to the structural thesis, use the current consolidation to rebalance toward higher-quality names with better risk/reward, and ensure the position is hedged against a broad risk-off scenario through portfolio-level diversification rather than trying to time the uranium-specific cycle. The Antifragile score of 65 suggests above-average but not maximum allocation — size for the thesis, not the euphoria.
